claims_disputed.claim: TAgent feedback drives refinement: 82.0% of 600 adjacent round transitions improve and 94.7% of runs finish R3 above R1.
claims_disputed.reason: The same TAgent rubric is both the feedback given to agents and the score; improvement on it is partly teaching-to-the-grader. There is no bare-retry or generic-feedback ablation to separate 'feedback content' from 'another round of time' (each round also gets up to 90 more minutes).

pattern_stance_changes.reason: QA-first ties with rotation (83.3) on the 10-project mean from essentially single runs with no variance. The paper itself says QA-first works by turning requirements into acceptance targets 'matching TAgent validation', so the advantage is confounded with alignment to the grader's rubric.
Rubric-compiled requirements are the evaluation instrument and the shared feedback for every mode, not a manipulated variable; nothing compares agents with and without structured acceptance criteria.

missed_issues: Selective reruns: non-IM projects are rerun 'only when experts flag a test as abnormal' (Limitations), an unblinded, outcome-dependent rerun policy.
Goodhart/benchmark_overfit: the grader's rubric feeds back into the agents each round, so final scores measure convergence to the grader as much as functional quality.
The contamination claim ('not sensitive to data contamination') is an assertion; the projects come from a capstone corpus 'since 2018', and the generated code is 'typically 2000+ lines of Python'.
Abstract says 'heavy managerial oversight degrades performance', yet the appendix lists PM oversight as the best mode on the crowdsourcing project (P02, 80.9).
note: The first review is accurate and appropriately skeptical (single runs, abstract–body mismatches, self-built grader). I only downgrade the QA-first/TDD and structured-requirements stances, which are confounded by the grader being the feedback source.
